title: TA8-14266
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, a citizen of Honduras, is seeking refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA).

The claimant fears the criminal gang known as the "M-18" or the "Mara Salvatrucha" in Honduras. The claimant started a small business in 1997. This business, according to the claimant, went well until XXXXX 2002, when he was approached by gang members to pay a monthly protection fee. According to the claimant, business people, taxi drivers, bus fare collectors and store owners are targeted by gang members to support their cause. The claimant also indicated that nobody is safe from the gangs in Honduras.

The claimant initially rejected the demands of the M-18. After realizing that the gang members were harassing his customers and the police told him they could not do much, he succumbed to the gang's demands and began paying them a monthly fee. In XXXXX 2003, the claimant could not make his monthly payment due to poor sales. He promised the gang members that he would pay the fee for XXXXX and XXXXX on XXXXX, 2003. In XXXXX 2003, the claimant was unable to make his full payments, as he had proposed to the gang. The gang members refused to accept his partial payment.

On XXXXX 2003, the claimant was physically assaulted, cut with a machete and shot seven times by gang members. The claimant was hospitalized and remained in a XXXXX XXXXX. The claimant's family received threatening messages, intended for the claimant, from the gang members while the claimant was in hospital. Once released from hospital, the claimant's family members approached the police seeking protection for the claimant. The police told the claimant's family members that they could not take responsibility for the claimant's security and suggested that he find a place to hide. The claimant went to stay with various family members and friends around Honduras. While in hiding, the claimant's family continued to be harassed by gang members looking for the claimant.

The claimant fled to Mexico on XXXXX 2005, where he remained until XXXXX, 2006 when he entered the United States of America (U.S.A.). The claimant remained in the U.S.A. until XXXXX 2008 when he entered Canada. On XXXXX, 2008, the claimant filed a claim for refugee protection.
The Board finds that the claimant is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. ANALYSIS Identity
The claimant's identity has been established through identity documents filed in evidence.2 Determinative Issues
The determinative issues are nexus, failure to claim in the U.S.A. and generalized risk. Nexus
The claimant fears members of the M-18 gang in Honduras. They have extorted him for money, and, when he failed to meet their extortion demands, he was physically assaulted and received threats.

He is, therefore, a victim of crime, which does not provide him with a nexus to one of the five Convention refugee grounds, namely, race, religion, nationality, real or imputed political opinion, or membership in a particular social group.
Accordingly, the claimant is not a Convention refugee and his claim under section 96 of the IRPA fails. The balance of the analysis is pursuant to section 97 of the IRPA. Failure to Claim Elsewhere

The claimant left Honduras in 2005 and remained in the U.S.A. for over three years before coming to Canada. The claimant acknowledged that he remained and worked in the U.S.A. illegally. He indicated that the situation for illegal immigrants in the U.S.A. was precarious and the risk of having problems with the authorities leading to deportation was very high. The claimant also indicated that he saw many families separated and hundreds of people deported because their claims for refugee protection were unsuccessful. The claimant's sister in the U.S.A. helped the claimant find information about Canada's refugee system. While the Board certainly does not condone the illegal status of the claimant in the U.S.A., he learned of the fate of others similarly situated to him and decided not to seek asylum in the U.S.A. for fear of being deported. When he became more concerned, he looked for a further option, which was to enter Canada. The Board, in this particular case, accepts his explanations for the sequence of events subsequent to his departure from Honduras. Generalized Risk

The claimant's fears arise out of extortion threats from the M-18 gang. They had been demanding money, and the claimant acceded to their demands. However, when he could not meet their monthly fee demands, he was physically assaulted and threatened with death. The claimant has indicated that no one in Honduras is safe from this gang.

The Board finds that the risk faced by the claimant in terms of extortion and associated violence is a risk faced generally by individuals who are perceived to have money, and is one that is faced by a large population in Honduras.

Section 97(1) of the IRPA states: A person in need of protection is a person in Canada whose removal to their country or countries of nationality or, if they do not have a country of nationality, their country of former habitual residence, would subject them personally (b) to a risk to their life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if (ii) the risk would be faced by the person in every part of that country and is not faced generally by other individuals in or from that country.

A number of decisions of the Board finding that the risk faced by the population of a country at the hands of the Mara Salvatrucha is a generalized one have been upheld by the Federal Court.3 In Ventura De Parada, the Court held that an increased risk experienced by a subcategory of the population is not personalized where that same risk is experienced by the whole generally, albeit at a reduced frequency.4

Documentary evidence5 indicates that the gang problem in Honduras is "endemic," and gang-related murders, carjackings and robberies are frequent. Gangs in Honduras impose "a war tax" on market and street vendors, on bus and taxi drivers, and on delivery trucks in what they call "their territory". The Maras have developed a "military and commercial structure" and they serve as "the workforce for drug trafficking, organized crime and local extortion of merchants". 93 percent of former gang members in Honduras stated that the Maras were hired by members of organized crime and by drug traffickers to carry out "special jobs," such as murders, drug sales and acts of vengeance.

Further documentary evidence indicates that the anti-Mara squad of the Honduran Community Police estimates that, in 2007, there were approximately 70,000 Mara members, including 800 leaders, 20,000 active members, 15,000 aspiring members or sympathizers, and 30,000 others who were either family members, collaborators or employers. A lack of resources and manpower causes local police to be "ineffective at deterring crime" and that response times are "often too slow". The National Preventive Police and the Criminal investigations Directorate General suffer from a "lack of manpower, training, equipment, low pay, and motivation". There is also a shortage of funds to purchase vehicles, fuel, radio equipment and maintenance services. The main measures taken by the police in Central America to combat gangs include arrest operations, investigations, patrol of sectors considered to be dangerous and the formation of anti-Mara groups. However, some police augment their meagre salaries with bribes from the Maras.

In this case, it is accepted that the claimant was subjected personally to a risk to his life. The gang physically assaulted him and threatened him with death if he did not accede to their demands for money.

In my opinion, having regard to all of the evidence including the documentary evidence before the panel, the risk faced by this claimant upon return to his country is one faced generally by many individuals in Honduras in terms of extortion from individuals who are perceived to have money. Extortion is part of the Maras' modus operandi and constitutes a widespread risk for all citizens who are working in Honduras. It particularly affects those individuals perceived to have money. Therefore, the Board finds that the claimant is not a person in need of protection.

The claimant is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Accordingly, this claim is rejected. (signed) "M. Pettinella" M.
